lesson.title: OpenFlow: Programming the Switch from the Outside
lesson.summary: OpenFlow is a standardized protocol that lets a centralized controller directly read and modify a switch's flow tables, making it possible to separate a network's control plane from its data plane in practice.
lesson.body:
In a traditional router or switch, the logic that decides where traffic should go and the mechanism that actually forwards it live inside the same box, often even on the same chip, running vendor specific software that a network operator has limited ability to change. That works, but it means every device in a network makes its own local decisions, using its own routing protocol implementation, and reprogramming network wide behavior means touching many devices individually. Software defined networking, or SDN, proposes a different structure: pull the decision making logic, the control plane, out of individual switches entirely, and centralize it in software running somewhere else, while switches keep only the fast, simple job of forwarding packets according to rules they are told to install.

OpenFlow is the protocol that makes this idea concrete and, importantly, standardized rather than proprietary. It defines a communication channel between a centralized controller and a switch, and a message format for the controller to inspect and modify the switch's flow tables directly. Each flow table entry pairs a match, a set of header fields like source and destination IP address, MAC address, TCP or UDP port, and VLAN tag, with an action, such as forward out a specific port, drop the packet, rewrite a header field, or send the packet up to the controller for inspection. Because this interface is standardized, a controller can, in principle, program switches from different hardware vendors using the same protocol, something that was difficult before OpenFlow existed.

A concrete walkthrough shows how this plays out. Suppose a new flow, the first packet of a new TCP connection, arrives at an OpenFlow switch and the switch's flow table has no entry matching it. Rather than guessing, the switch encapsulates the packet in a message called packet-in and sends it to the controller. The controller, which holds a view of the broader network (a role covered in more detail in the next chapter), computes where this flow should go, perhaps balancing load across several paths, and sends flow-mod messages back to the switch, and possibly to other switches along the chosen path, installing the matching rule. From that point forward, every subsequent packet in that same flow is matched and forwarded entirely within the switch's data plane, at full line rate, without involving the controller again. Only the first packet paid the cost of a decision. Every packet after it just gets forwarded.

This is the practical realization of the split between control plane and data plane. The switch's hardware stays simple and fast. The complex decision making software runs centrally, where it can see more of the network and be updated without touching every device by hand. OpenFlow does not do anything a switch could not technically do before. What it changes is who gets to decide the rules, and how easily those rules can be reprogrammed.
